scope: One consecutive record; full stored text, registered 1280x720 native/mobile image, mortgage-affordability arithmetic and official-statistic checks

title.analysis: How Much Home You Can ACTUALLY Afford is a plain affordability question with one capitalized intensifier (ACTUALLY) that implies the viewer's current estimate is wrong. It names no salary, price or year, no 'shocking' or 'math is brutal' tag, and no number to self-locate against, so it is the least specific packaging in the channel's affordability family. Observed same-channel contrasts: How Much House Your Salary Actually Buys You (WyHZdWkS85U, 2026-02-19) is near-identical in meaning but adds 'Your Salary' and reached 7.75752x STRONG; its car twin How Much Car Your Salary Actually Buys You (Shocking) (jxeB_FcQrc0) published two days before this video reached 3.9618x STRONG. Who Can Actually Afford a $500K House in 2026 (The Math Is Brutal) (1mIp0mUyCKU) reached 23.00921x STRONG, but the same template with other prices was weak or typical: $250k (N2HdBntwQGU) 0.37031x WEAK and $750K (S_8SLGjLrBM) 0.56895x TYPICAL. Other housing-pain titles: Why So Many Homeowners Are Going Broke in 2025 (Zw038izB1tg, eight days earlier) 2.19528x STRONG, versus The 50 Year Mortgage Trap (gwm1Hr5iipU) 0.32481x WEAK and The 'Hidden' Costs (The Homeowner Nightmare) (GZUH1m8INNs) 0.48648x WEAK. This video sits at 0.58202x TYPICAL (ten-peer) and 0.20716x WEAK (five-peer). The contrast with the salary-framed twins is consistent with, but does not prove, the idea that a personal anchor (your salary) or a concrete price helps; the template-level spread ($500K STRONG versus $250K WEAK) shows that wording alone does not determine outcome.
title.search_demand: Classic evergreen search query ('how much house can I afford') with heavy calculator and lender competition in search results; historical query volume, impressions and traffic sources unavailable.
title.script_alignment: Partly aligned. The script never gives a method or formula for the viewer's own number; it walks through rules (28%, 1% maintenance, 45% DTI, '30-30-30') and mostly argues that the answer is 'less than you think' and that renting may be better. 'ACTUALLY' is paid off as a reality check, not as a personal answer.

thumbnail.analysis: Registered maxresdefault fetched fresh and inspected at native 1280x720 and proportional 320x180. Pure white background. Left third: a cartoon man drawn in an adult-animation style (large egg-shaped head, short brown hair, half-lidded flat or skeptical expression, prominent chin, white short-sleeved button shirt, black belt with gold buckle, blue jeans) pointing right with his index finger. This is not the ginger-haired hoodie presenter seen in the NICK_133 image; whether it is a recurring channel character is not established here. Upper right: very large black condensed type 'THE 28% RULE' on two lines. Lower right: a grey two-storey suburban house illustration with a large orange-to-red dollar sign with a red glow overlaid in front of it, and a thick black curved arrow from the right edge pointing at the house. Hierarchy: '28% RULE' first, then the glowing dollar sign, then the character. At 320px '28% RULE' and 'THE' stay fully legible with strong black-on-white contrast; the house and glowing dollar sign still read clearly as 'housing cost'; the character's facial expression becomes small but the pointing gesture remains readable. Relationship to title and script: the image and title say different things. The title asks how much you can afford; the image names a specific rule, which the script introduces at about character 2,617 and then argues is outdated, while also covering a '30-30-30 rule', 1% maintenance and 45% DTI. The image therefore promises a single rule the script mainly rejects, and contains no affordability number or salary anchor. The red glowing dollar sign is the only warning cue; no fear text. Historical edits and any A/B testing are unverified; image performance contribution is not measured.

script.opening_words: You know that moment when you're scrolling through Zillow at 2:00 in the morning looking at houses you'll never be able to afford, wondering if the universe is playing some sort of cosmic joke on you? Yeah, we've all been there.
script.ending_words: If this video saved you from a financial disaster or just made you feel better about renting that apartment with the interpretive dance neighbor, hit that like button and subscribe for more reality checks that might crush your dreams, but save your bank account.
script.analysis: Full 19,118 canonical characters read in two contiguous chunks (0-10,000 and 10,000-19,118). The hook is a relatable late-night scene (scrolling Zillow at 2 AM, a $500,000 three-bedroom, a mortgage calculator 'like a freight train carrying student loan debt'), which is specific and self-identifying, but the presenter intro and subscribe ask arrive within about 150 words, before any promise of what the viewer will learn. The thesis ('the old rules don't really work anymore') is stated at character ~1,000, then the script spends most of its length on cost categories rather than a method. Structure is cumulative rather than escalating: rule critique, cost list, $80K worked example, DTI and credit, down payment and closing costs, $80K example again, rent versus buy, a second 'rule' critique, a $100K stretch example, close. Transitions lean on stock phrases ('Here's where things get interesting', 'Here's where the math gets really fun', 'Here's where the math starts getting really interesting', 'Here's the thing that really gets me', 'But here's where this gets really entertaining'); they signal novelty but rarely open a real question, and the repetition is noticeable. Two blocks are near-duplicates: the 1% maintenance rule on a $500,000 house ($5,000/year, over $400/month) is given at ~4,700 and repeated almost verbatim at ~14,000, and the 'bell bottoms / internet was a fad' joke appears at ~2,900 and again at ~16,100. Comedic similes are dense (amusement park with broken rides, bathtub with a teaspoon, Everest versus helicopter, yoga instructors on steroids); they keep tone light but often replace a number where one is needed. The strongest writing is the concrete worked examples ($10,000/month gross versus $7,000 take-home; $100,000 income at 50% of gross leaving about $800), which convert abstract ratios into what is left for food. Main weakness: the title question is never answered for the viewer; no step-by-step calculation of their own affordable price is given, the example arithmetic contains internal inconsistencies (see claim audit), and the close ('the math doesn't lie') is asserted rather than earned. All stored text read; not an original-audio, editing or retention verification.

beat_map.beat: Zillow-at-2AM hook, mortgage-calculator reality check, presenter intro and subscribe ask framed as saving you from a terrible decision
'Old rules don't work in 2025' thesis, income-times-magic-number strawman, and what-you-can-afford versus what-a-bank-will-lend distinction ($700,000 approval example)
28% gross-income rule introduced and attacked as outdated (bell bottoms, $400 car payments, $200 phone bills, subscriptions)
Renting versus owning cost structure: property tax, insurance, maintenance, HOA, lawnmower; 1% maintenance rule on $500,000 = $5,000/year, over $400/month
$80,000 median-income worked example: 28% = about $1,800/month, roughly $250,000 house with 20% down at 7%, $50,000 down payment; median home over $400,000; risky workarounds; 6-month emergency fund
Debt-to-income (45% cap), lender meeting, credit score (50 points = 6% versus 7%), gross versus take-home, $10,000/month example with $4,500 debt payments
Down payment (20% of $500,000 = $100,000), 3% down 'immediately underwater', closing costs 2-5%, property tax 0.5-2%, homeowners insurance $1,500-$3,000
$80,000 example revisited with taxes/insurance/maintenance ($1,400 mortgage becomes over $2,000, 'closer to 35%'), maintenance and big-ticket repairs
Rent-is-cheaper-in-most-markets claim ($3,000 rent versus $4,000 own), slow early equity, $100,000 down-payment opportunity cost at 7-10% versus 7% mortgage
Repeated 'parents' era' rant, '30-30-30 rule' (3x income, 30% cash, 30% of gross), $75,000 -> $225,000, people stretching to 40-50%, $100,000 income at 50% of gross leaving about $800
Recap ('the math doesn't lie'), banks are not your financial therapists, like/subscribe close

claim_audit: $10,000/month example: narrator says a lender may approve $4,500 of debt payments, take-home is about $7,000, $4,500 is 'almost 2/3' of take-home, and 'that leaves you with $1,500'. Calculation: $4,500 / $7,000 = 64.3% (so 'almost 2/3' is right), but $7,000 - $4,500 = $2,500, not $1,500. Arithmetic error in the narrator's claim (ASR misrecognition of 'twenty-five hundred' is possible but not verified against audio).

$80,000 revisited: narrator says a 'mortgage payment of maybe $1,400' becomes 'over $2,000' with taxes, insurance and maintenance, so 'you're spending closer to 35% of your gross income'. Calculation: $2,000 / ($80,000 / 12 = $6,667) = 30.0%; 35% would require about $2,333/month. The '$1,400' is consistent with principal and interest on a $200,000 loan at 7% for 30 years ($1,330.60). Also, the 28% rule as stated applies to total housing costs, so the script first treats $1,800 as the housing budget, then as the mortgage alone; the two uses are inconsistent.

'$1,800 a month might get you a mortgage on a house worth about $250,000 assuming 20% down and a 7% rate': 28% of $80,000 / 12 = $1,866.67 (about $1,800, slightly rounded down). $250,000 with 20% down is a $200,000 loan, $1,330.60 principal and interest at 7%; if the full $1,800 went to principal and interest, it would support about $338,000 with 20% down. The $250,000 figure is plausible only if roughly $470/month is reserved for taxes and insurance, which the script does not say at that point. The 7% assumption was above the actual market: Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year fixed averaged 6.23% on 2025-11-26, the day before publication (a $200,000 loan at 6.23% is $1,228.83).

'$80,000 a year puts you right around the median household income': Census reported 2023 real median household income of $80,610 (September 2024 release, available before publication); verified through syndicated coverage of the Census release, not the Census table itself. A 2024 figure released in September 2025 would also have been available before publication but was not checked here (UNVERIFIED).

'Median priced home in America costs over $400,000': FRED MSPUS (Census/HUD median sales price of houses sold) shows Q3 2025 at $410,100 in a February 2026 vintage (Q2 2025 at $410,800 in the July 2025 vintage, available before publication). Claim holds. Calculation: with 20% down at 6.23%, a $320,000 loan is $1,966/month principal and interest alone, about 29.5% of $80,000 gross before tax and insurance, so 'the median earner cannot afford the median home under 28%' holds directionally.

'Most lenders want total monthly debt payments ... no more than 45% of gross': Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-6-02 sets 36% for manually underwritten loans, up to 45% with credit-score and reserve requirements, and up to 50% for loans underwritten through Desktop Underwriter. '45%' is one real cap, but 'most lenders ... no more than 45%' understates the 50% automated-underwriting limit; FHA rules were not checked.

'A difference of just 50 points on your credit score can mean the difference between a 6% and a 7% interest rate': not verified against a rate-by-score table (UNVERIFIED); a full percentage point for 50 points is likely at the high end. Calculation: on a $400,000 loan the 6% versus 7% difference is $263/month, about $94,700 over 30 years, so 'tens of thousands' is correct if the spread were that large.

'Put down as little as 3% ... you're immediately underwater ... you owe more than the house is worth before you've even moved in': with 3% down the loan is 97% of the purchase price, so the borrower does not owe more than the purchase price at signing. Being underwater on a net-of-selling-costs basis, or after a price decline, is possible, but the literal claim is incorrect.

Supporting arithmetic checked and correct: 20% of $500,000 = $100,000; closing costs 2-5% of $500,000 = $10,000-$25,000; property tax 0.5%-2% of $500,000 = $2,500-$10,000/year, and $10,000/12 = $833 ('over $800 per month'); 1% maintenance = $5,000/year = $416.67/month ('over $400'); 3 x $75,000 = $225,000; $100,000 income, about $70,000 take-home = $5,833/month, minus $5,000 = $833 ('$800'). The 2-5% closing-cost, 0.5-2% property-tax and $1,500-$3,000 insurance ranges were not checked against a primary source.

Rule names and history: the commonly cited form of the second rule is '30/30/3' (housing at most 30% of gross, 30% of the home's value in cash, home price at most 3x income); the narrator calls it '30-30-30' while describing a 3x term, a likely naming error (possible ASR effect). The claim that the 28% rule dates from the bell-bottom era and that 'wages have basically stayed the same' is unsourced and not verified here.

Rent versus buy: 'in most markets across America right now, it's actually cheaper to rent than to buy' is presented as fact with no source (UNVERIFIED in this review). The $3,000 rent versus $4,000 own comparison is hypothetical. Early equity claim: first-month principal on a 7% 30-year mortgage is $163.94 on $200,000 and $327.88 on $400,000, consistent with 'a few hundred dollars'. Opportunity-cost claim that investing a $100,000 down payment at 7-10% versus paying 7% mortgage interest is 'essentially breaking even' omits that market returns are uncertain while the mortgage rate is fixed; historical 7-10% return range not sourced.

Possible ASR artefacts preserved, not corrected against audio: 'wore bell bottoms on ironically' (likely 'unironically'), 'and and boom', 'instead of trying to sell you borrowing half a million dollars is a totally reasonable life decision' (sentence fragment), 'if you change your minds', and the '$1,500' figure noted above.

topic.analysis: Housing affordability and rent-versus-buy for first-time buyers. Evergreen with a 2025 rate and price backdrop; beginner audience; very high household relevance. Mechanisms covered: front-end housing ratio, total debt-to-income, gross versus take-home income, non-mortgage ownership costs (tax, insurance, maintenance, closing), down payment and PMI, credit-score pricing, and opportunity cost of the down payment. Distinctive audience question: 'On my income, what price can I safely buy, and is renting smarter?' The video answers the second half (renting may be cheaper) far more than the first.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Original opportunity: a reconciled, step-by-step affordability walk-through at a few incomes using a dated, sourced mortgage rate (for example Freddie Mac PMMS for the publication week), sourced median income and price, and a take-home-based budget, showing price ceilings under 28% of gross, 36%/45%/50% DTI and a take-home-based rule side by side. Keep the gross-versus-take-home worked examples and the 'bank approval is not affordability' framing, which are the strongest elements; remove repeated blocks and fix the example arithmetic.

virality.analysis: Observed result: 24,068 frozen views at 287.5763 days; ten-peer ratio 0.58202x TYPICAL and five-peer ratio 0.20716x WEAK, both independently reproduced. The tier is peer-sensitive: it is TYPICAL against ten age peers and WEAK against the nearest five, because three of the closer peers (jxeB_FcQrc0 3.9618x, Tg_n8zGC7qw 3.61009x, iAgCkciSMDs 3.35391x) were STRONG. Evidence-backed interpretation: in the same week, the channel's salary-anchored car video (jxeB_FcQrc0, two days earlier) reached about 5.9x this video's views, and a later near-identical housing title with 'Your Salary' (WyHZdWkS85U) was STRONG, so this topic was not inherently weak on this channel; the difference lies somewhere in packaging, timing, or content, which public views cannot separate. Hypotheses: (a) the generic title with no salary or price anchor gave less reason to click than salary-anchored siblings; (b) the thumbnail's '28% RULE' promise conflicted with the title's 'how much can I afford' question; (c) repetition and lack of a personal answer reduced satisfaction. None is measurable without impressions, CTR, traffic sources or retention. Proposed experiment: in owned content, test the same affordability script under a salary-anchored title versus a generic title, and a rule-named thumbnail versus a salary/price-number thumbnail, measuring CTR and retention through the worked-example segment. Engagement proxies: 613 likes (2.55% of views) and 124 comments (0.52%).
virality.observed_result: 24,068 views; 613 likes; 124 comments; 1,192 seconds; 0.58202x TYPICAL ten-peer / 0.20716x WEAK five-peer (peer-sensitive tier). Public metrics only.

virality.format_fit: 19:52 long-form narrated essay (visual format not reviewed); comedic simile-heavy narration over worked examples; runtime is not watch time.
virality.channel_context: Below the ten-peer median and well below the nearest five peers in a November 2025 cluster where salary- and wealth-threshold titles outperformed; later same-channel housing titles with explicit salary or $500K anchors outperformed strongly.
alternative_explanations: Packaging hypothesis: no salary or price anchor in the title and a thumbnail promising a single '28% rule' may have attracted fewer clicks than salary-anchored siblings; CTR and impressions unavailable.
Timing hypothesis: Thanksgiving Day upload and a dense week of same-channel uploads (one video per day in the peer window) may have split audience attention; traffic data unavailable.
Satisfaction hypothesis: repeated blocks and no personal affordability answer may have weakened viewing; retention unavailable.
Confounders: algorithmic exploration, unknown later title or thumbnail edits, and the peer window drawn from a single dense upload cluster.

original_content_lesson.test: Produce an original affordability explainer that gives the viewer a computed price ceiling at several incomes with a dated sourced rate, and test salary-anchored versus generic titles and number-led versus rule-led thumbnails in owned experiments; measure CTR, retention at the worked-example segment, and comments asking for personal calculations.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH for arithmetic reproduction and stored-text claim conflicts; MEDIUM for official-statistic checks via search excerpts; LOW for causal virality attribution.

event.linkage: No dated event or historical search series is linked; evergreen topic with a contemporaneous rate backdrop noted only for claim checking.

review_process: Drafted by a read-only research subagent that read the full stored text and inspected the actual image; coordinator gate verified identity, image hash/dimensions, verbatim opening/ending words, contiguous read and beat ranges, age-peer listing and reproduced ratios; coordinator spot-checks: thumbnail matched (THE 28% RULE, house, red dollar); $1,500 remainder and 35% quotes verbatim; 7,000-4,500=2,500 arithmetic confirmed.
